newsitem.title: CANADA: FUSARIUM HITS 10 PCT OF MANITOBA WHEAT - AG CANADA.
newsitem.headline: FUSARIUM HITS 10 PCT OF MANITOBA WHEAT - AG CANADA.

text.p: Fusarium headblight has infected 10 percent of Manitoba's wheat crop, an Agriculture Canada scientist said Wednesday.

"About 10 percent of Manitoba's wheat crop has fusarium headblight, and western Manitoba south of Brandon in the Boissevain and Killarney areas were particularly severe," said Andy Tekauz, head of Agriculture Canada's cereal disease section at Winnipeg's Cereal Research Centre.
"This is fairly close to 1993 when we saw about C$70 million in yield loss," Tekauz said in an interview.

The fusarium, or scab, fungus is caused by prolonged rain during heading. It can produce vomitoxin, which in high concentrations in feed wheat can cause nausea in animals. Southwest Manitoba has seen nine inches of rain since August 1.
The fungus spread west outside the Red River Valley for the second consecutive year, CWB weather and crop surveillance director Paul Bullock said.
Some of the infected regions saw hot, humid weather but no rain.
"If heavy dews are enough to bring the disease out in vulnerable crops, that's a problem," Bullock said. "There's no chemical for it. This is a crop breeding problem."
Canada Prairie Spring wheats and durum wheats are most vulnerable to fusarium headblight, he said.
Agriculture Canada expects to have a fusarium-resistant wheat on the market by 2001 with the first fusarium-resistant hard red spring wheat out by 2002, Ag Canada's Tekauz said.
